cue: Describing a typical score when there are no extreme scores.
formula: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{x}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>sum of the scores</mtext><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{sum of the scores}}{n}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: One extreme score (an outlier) pulls the mean toward it; the median does not move much.

front: The median: half the scores are below it, half above.
cue: A typical score when the distribution is skewed (incomes, reaction times).
formula: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>median</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{median}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>the middle score in order</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{the middle score in order}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Put the scores in order first; with an even count, average the two middle scores.

front: The mode: the score that occurs most often.
cue: Categories (favorite color) or the peak of a distribution.
formula: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>mode</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{mode}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>the most frequent score</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{the most frequent score}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: A distribution can have two modes (bimodal); the mode is a score, not how often it occurs.

front: The range: the distance from the lowest score to the highest.
trap: One outlier makes the range huge; it uses only two scores.

front: The standard deviation: the typical distance of scores from the mean.
cue: Comparing how spread out two groups are; reading the normal curve.
trap: A larger SD means more spread, not higher scores. The exam asks you to read and interpret it, not to compute it from a long list.

front: A z score: how many standard deviations a score is from the mean.
cue: Comparing scores from different tests, or placing a score on the normal curve.
trap: Below the mean, z is negative. Subtract the mean first, then divide by the SD.

front: The 68-95-99.7 rule for a normal distribution.
cue: The share of people between two scores, or above or below one.
formula: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>68</mn><mo>%</mo><mtext> within </mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext> SD</mtext><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">68\% \text{ within } 1\text{ SD},</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mspace width="0.2778em"></mspace><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo><mtext> within </mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\; 95\% \text{ within } 2,</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mspace width="0.2778em"></mspace><mn>99.7</mn><mo>%</mo><mtext> within </mtext><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\; 99.7\% \text{ within } 3</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Half of 68% (34%) lies on each side of the mean; the bands are 34, 13.5, 2.35 and 0.15 percent.

front: A percentile rank: the percent of a group who scored lower.
cue: Interpreting a score: the 84th percentile beats 84% of the group.
formula: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>percentile rank</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{percentile rank}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>percent of scores below</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{percent of scores below}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: A percentile is not a percent correct. One SD above the mean is about the 84th percentile (50 + 34).

front: The correlation coefficient r: the direction (sign) and strength (closeness to 1 or -1) of a straight-line relationship.
cue: Describing a scatterplot or a correlational study.
formula: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>≤</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1 \le r \le +1</annotation></semantics></math>
worked: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mtext> for </mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r \text{ for } (1,2),(2,4),(3,6)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 1</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Correlation is not causation: a third variable may explain both. A negative r is as strong as a positive one of the same size.

front: Statistical significance: a difference this large would rarely happen by chance alone if the variables were unrelated.
cue: Reading an experiment's results: is the difference between groups likely real?
trap: Significant does not mean large or important; effect size says how big the difference is.
